title: The Comeback Kid

jokes.text: Leslie dramatically builds up her campaign manager announcement with a self-provided drum roll, then names Ann Perkins
jokes.setup: Leslie hypes this as a 'huge job' requiring 'late-night one-on-one jam sessions' and makes everyone wait for a drum roll she performs herself
jokes.punchline: The grand reveal is Ann — her best friend with zero political experience — while Tom dryly confirms 'Yep'
jokes.explanation: Classic Leslie move — over-the-top ceremony for a dubious choice. The self-supplied drum roll is perfectly in character. Tom's flat 'Yep' as background punctuation is a nice deadpan touch. The setup earns the reveal.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ann, you're like a tropical fish. You're so vibrant and colorful, and you brighten up any room you're in. You're just... you're a tropical fish.

jokes.text: Ann, you beautiful tropical fish. You're smart as a whip and you're cool under pressure. You've resuscitated a human heart in your bare hands. No, I haven't. You haven't? No. You will. You're that good of a nurse.
jokes.setup: Leslie flatters Ann with escalating, increasingly bizarre compliments to convince her to take the job
jokes.punchline: Leslie confidently asserts Ann has 'resuscitated a human heart in her bare hands,' Ann corrects her, and Leslie doubles down by saying 'You will' — treating a future hypothetical as qualification
jokes.explanation: One of the best Leslie compliment sequences in the series. 'Beautiful tropical fish' is already a great non-sequitur, but the resuscitation beat is exceptional: Leslie invents a credential, gets corrected, and instead of backing down, converts it into a future prediction delivered with total sincerity. This is pure Leslie — her love for Ann is so intense it overcomes logic. The 'You will' deserves its near-legendary status. Character integration score is a 9 because no other character on television could deliver this.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ann, you're such an amazing nurse. You've performed so many successful surgeries.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Leslie, I'm not a surgeon. I've never performed a surgery.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, you will. Because you're that good.

jokes.text: What about Ben? / Ben is poison to my campaign. Our relationship is the reason why my advisors pulled out.
jokes.setup: Ann logically suggests Ben, who actually ran a campaign successfully at age 18
jokes.punchline: Leslie describes Ben as 'poison' with the kind of dramatic certainty usually reserved for villains, then delivers 'pulled out' with complete obliviousness to the double entendre
jokes.explanation: The 'pulled out' double entendre works because Leslie is totally unaware of it, which is in character. Not a showstopper but a solid mid-tier moment.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I literally just started this job yesterday.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: And you're already terrible at it.

jokes.text: Don't listen to your head or your heart. Just look at my eyes and say yes.
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to get Ann to agree to be campaign manager
jokes.punchline: The instruction to ignore both reason and emotion and instead just stare into Leslie's eyes is so intense it crosses into parody of persuasion
jokes.explanation: A tight, well-constructed line that captures Leslie's charismatic steamroller personality. The economy is excellent — three clauses that escalate the absurdity perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Hey Leslie, I just wanted to let you know that I clogged the toilet at home with some stuff I shouldn't have, and now there's water all over the bathroom floor, and I think I broke the sink trying to fix it.

jokes.text: And your first job as my campaign manager is to start dressing like one. / Again? You just hired me eight seconds ago. / Wow, you're doing a really bad job.
jokes.setup: Ann has literally just agreed eight seconds earlier
jokes.punchline: Leslie already has performance criticisms, and when Ann points out the impossibly short timeframe, Leslie turns it back on Ann as evidence of incompetence
jokes.explanation: A beautifully structured three-beat exchange. The timing of 'eight seconds' is precise and funny, but the real brilliance is Leslie's comeback — she weaponizes Ann's own logical objection as proof of the objection's validity. Tight, in-character, highly quotable. Just below the 8-anchor threshold but earns its score.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We don't need professional campaign managers. Running a campaign is just like committing murder — you plan it out, you execute it, and then you cover your tracks.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, that's a terrible analogy. Scratch that.

jokes.text: ANDY: Leslie? I tried to make ramen in the coffee pot and I broke everything.
jokes.setup: Leslie is mid-brag to her departing professional campaign managers about her 'brilliant, amazing' new advisory team being 'real killers'
jokes.punchline: Andy immediately undercuts her credibility by wandering in to report he destroyed the coffee pot attempting to make ramen
jokes.explanation: Structurally perfect comedic juxtaposition. Leslie calls her team 'real killers' and in the same breath Andy proves them to be anything but. The specific detail of 'ramen in the coffee pot' is wonderfully stupid — it's not just that Andy caused destruction, it's the particular domestic incompetence on display. The timing is impeccable and the joke requires zero setup beyond what's already in the scene.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It's like... it's like if someone murdered your best friend, and then they tried to be your best friend. You wouldn't just—okay, that analogy isn't working.

jokes.text: Are most murders committed by highly-trained, professional assassins? No. They're committed by friends and co-workers.
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to reassure herself (in a talking head) that not having professional campaign managers is fine
jokes.punchline: She uses murder statistics as a metaphor for grassroots campaigning, then has to concede the analogy was 'way better in my head'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The murder analogy is absurd but internally logical — Leslie is genuinely trying to make a point about amateur passion beating professional polish. The self-aware beat of 'that analogy was way better in my head' is a perfect topper that both acknowledges the dark wrongness and preserves Leslie's essential optimism. It's structured in two parts across two timestamps, which amplifies the impact. Highly quotable and distinctly Parks and Rec in its cheerful wrongness.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Well, his name is Champion.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: So he's the champion.

jokes.text: That analogy was way better in my head. (DOOR SQUEAKING) (BELL JINGLING)
jokes.setup: Leslie has just delivered the murder/friends analogy and realized how it sounded
jokes.punchline: The self-deprecating admission followed by immediately moving on — the squeaking door and bell suggest she exits with forced confidence
jokes.explanation: The topper to the murder joke. Counted separately because the pause and self-awareness beat add an additional laugh. The sound design (door squeak, bell) implies a comic exit that sells the moment.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Champion's lost a leg, but he's still got three good ones. He can run, he can jump, he can play fetch...

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: The only thing he can't do is... well, he can't lick his own butt anymore.

jokes.text: That is a three-legged dog. His name is Champion, because he's the Dog World Champion.
jokes.setup: Andy and April have brought home a dog, revealed to have only three legs
jokes.punchline: The name 'Champion' is given precisely because of his disability, with Andy's logic being completely sincere and circular
jokes.explanation: The introduction of Champion is a great character moment for Andy. The name is funny because it's both ironic and sincere simultaneously — Andy genuinely means it. Sets up a running gag for the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: April, you can decide what we do with the dog. I'm putting this completely in your hands.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Okay. I've made my decision. We're going to have to put him down. Take him out back, and shoot him in the head.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa! April, no!

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You said I could decide.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I thought you'd pick something like... I don't know, a name or something.

jokes.text: He can do more with three legs than most dogs can do with four. Except for digging. He's really bad at digging.
jokes.setup: Andy is making a rousing case for Champion's superiority despite having three legs
jokes.punchline: The triumphant defense collapses immediately with the specific, practical caveat about digging
jokes.explanation: The structure is excellent: a broad inspiring claim immediately punctured by a specific practical failure. The specificity of 'digging' is what makes it work — it's such a mundane, observable dog activity. Andy delivers it without irony, which makes it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Yeah, we have jobs. Unlike you.

jokes.text: Champion goes back to the pound where he can be put down and killed forever.
jokes.setup: Andy is reassuring April (or Ron?) that they'll defer to the household decision-maker's wishes about the dog
jokes.punchline: The euphemism escalates from 'go back to the pound' all the way to 'put down and killed forever' — as if Andy is trying to make the threat as vivid as possible to get sympathy
jokes.explanation: The redundant escalation 'put down AND killed forever' is great — 'killed forever' is not a thing, but Andy saying it reveals he's emotionally manipulating the situation while pretending to be reasonable.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: See? Hawaiian shirts are in. I told you.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Tom, I was making fun of you.

jokes.text: Ann got local hero Pistol Pete Disellio to endorse me... In 1992, Pistol Pete's last-second dunk against Eagleton High clinched a comeback victory for the Pawnee Central Drunken Savages. Team mascot later changed.
jokes.setup: Leslie is explaining who Pistol Pete is and why he matters
jokes.punchline: The team name 'Drunken Savages' is dropped with casual pride, followed by the dry parenthetical 'Team mascot later changed' — implying the name was changed for obvious reasons but Leslie doesn't feel the need to explain why
jokes.explanation: Classic Parks and Rec Pawnee world-building humor. The 'Drunken Savages' name is perfect small-town absurdism, and the throwaway 'Team mascot later changed' is a masterwork of economy — it implies an entire embarrassing history in four words without belaboring the joke.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That wasn't me, that was Champion.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Champion, you can't talk to people like that.

jokes.text: Tom's red carpet lifestyle confessional: My entire apartment is red carpet. On top of that, leading into my bedroom? A second red carpet. Oh, what's this in my shoe? Red carpet insole. Everywhere I go, I'm walking on red carpet.
jokes.setup: Tom is explaining how to make an event classy on a budget: a red carpet
jokes.punchline: The revelation that Tom lives entirely on red carpet, escalating to the red carpet insole — he has fully committed to the bit in his personal life
jokes.explanation: A genuinely funny escalating confessional. The red carpet insole is the best beat — it's so committed and so specific. Tom's delusion about his own fabulousness is perfectly embodied here. The 'Oh, what's this in my shoe?' theatrical reveal is a great comedic structure.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I don't want to generalize, but I've noticed that every single woman in this office is completely incompetent.

jokes.text: Also making a comeback, the casual Hawaiian shirt. / Well, well, well. Look who's ahead of the curve. / I was joking. You should soak that in bleach and burn it.
jokes.setup: Ann is listing comeback stories as campaign theme inspiration, including Rocky, RDJ, the Terminator
jokes.punchline: She adds the Hawaiian shirt as a joke, Tom takes it as a serious compliment to his (presumably terrible) shirt, and Ann has to clarify with a brutal fashion verdict
jokes.explanation: Works well as a quick character beat. Tom's vanity is established efficiently and Ann's deadpan destruction of it ('soak that in bleach and burn it') is sharp. The visual of the shirt adds to the comedy even unseen.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Here, try this calzone.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: No thanks. Do you know how many calories are in that? The sodium content alone could stop a human heart. Plus, it's fried in what I can only assume is liquefied saturated fat. I'm going to go eat a mound of steamed vegetables and then do 200 sit-ups.

jokes.text: The Terminator. He said, 'I'll be back,' and he was.
jokes.setup: Ann is listing impressive comeback stories to frame the campaign theme
jokes.punchline: The Terminator is included with a completely sincere factual justification — 'he said he'd be back, and he was' — treating a fictional robot villain as a legitimate political inspiration
jokes.explanation: The deadpan literalism of applying the Terminator's catchphrase as evidence of a comeback works well. Not a huge laugh but a solid chuckle — the economy of the explanation is what makes it.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Ben seems like he's really engaged with his hobbies, you know? He's got his model trains, he's building things in the garage. I think he's in a really good place right now.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Actually, I'm worried Ben might be severely depressed.

jokes.text: APRIL: (IN A MANLY VOICE) Shut up, Ann. I told you never to talk to me. (GASPS) That was Champion. Oh, my God. I'm sorry. Bad dog.
jokes.setup: Ann asks April about the venue rental; April clearly doesn't want to deal with Ann
jokes.punchline: April barks at Ann in a 'manly voice' and then immediately pretends it was the dog Champion, feigning shock and scolding him
jokes.explanation: Wonderfully stupid and perfectly April. The commitment required to (a) do a man voice, (b) blame the dog, and (c) 'scold' the dog is exactly April's brand of passive-aggressive weirdness. The structure is tight: offense, misdirection, fake accountability. Earns an 8 for character integration alone.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ann, you googled what campaign managers wear? That's so smart!

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Thanks, I wanted to look professional.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm impressed. Usually when you google something, it's like 'how to get a stain out of white pants' or 'why do my feet hurt.'

jokes.text: I don't want to paint with a broad brush here, but every single contractor in the world is a miserable, incompetent thief.
jokes.setup: Leslie wanted to hire a contractor; Ron volunteered to build the stage himself
jokes.punchline: Ron prefaces a sweeping, total condemnation with 'I don't want to paint with a broad brush here' — the qualifier being hilariously inapplicable to what follows
jokes.explanation: A top-tier Ron Swanson joke. The comedy is entirely in the gap between the hedge ('I don't want to paint with a broad brush') and the absolute, all-encompassing condemnation that follows. The hedge makes it funnier — it shows Ron believes he's being measured and fair. Deeply in character and highly quotable. The follow-up cooking detail (crimping calzone with a fork) is also funny as a visual non-sequitur.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: So you've been in the carpet business a long time?

dialogue.speaker: Carpet Salesman
dialogue.line: About thirty years.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That's impressive. You must really know how to lay it down.

dialogue.speaker: Carpet Salesman
dialogue.line: Well, yes, I've installed thousands of carpets.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I bet you're really good at getting it in tight spaces.

dialogue.speaker: Carpet Salesman
dialogue.line: It takes practice, but yes.

jokes.text: Ben is making calzones in an Italian accent: 'Or as you Americans like to say, calzones.'
jokes.setup: Ben is teaching himself to make calzones as a hobby while depressed; Chris visits and Ben introduces the food
jokes.punchline: Ben does a mock-Italian accent, calling them something else, then 'translates' to the same word — the accent version and the American version are identical
jokes.explanation: A decent absurdist bit — the accent is a non-joke that Ben commits to, which is funnier than if the punchline had a real punchline. The self-delusion of a depressed person investing in hobbies is the real comedy engine here.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Even his shoe insoles are red carpet for maximum luxury

jokes.text: Chris: 'I find calzone fatty and unnecessary.' (Beat) 'So you've hit a bit of a rough patch. And I care about you.'
jokes.setup: Chris declines Ben's calzone offer with a very Chris-specific critique, then pivots to emotional concern
jokes.punchline: The pivot from food criticism to emotional intervention — the calzone is 'fatty and unnecessary,' which functions as almost a metaphor for Ben's hobby — is jarring and funny
jokes.explanation: Chris's food opinions are always funnier for how absolute they are ('fatty and unnecessary' rather than just 'unhealthy'). The pivot to concern works because Chris is oblivious to how the transition sounds.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Can I sit on your lap instead of April's?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: No, Tom. If I let you do that, then I'd have to let Champion sit up front too.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: And I treat that three-legged dog like it has equal rights to car seating.

jokes.text: Ben excitedly shows Chris his claymation video, a hobby he's taken up while depressed. 'Isn't this just so cool?'
jokes.setup: Ben insists he's doing great and learning hobbies; he shows Chris his claymation as proof
jokes.punchline: The enthusiasm with which Ben presents the claymation, contrasted with Chris's strained reaction, sets up the later reveal that the video is catastrophically short
jokes.explanation: Functions as setup for the bigger claymation payoff later. Chris's 'It is so cool!' delivered while clearly alarmed is a good reaction beat. Moderate score as this is scene-building rather than a standalone joke.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Okay, so I kissed the dog, and it was pretty good. Then I kissed April, also very good. And then I kissed myself in the mirror, and... I gotta be honest, I'm in third place.

jokes.text: Chris Traeger (talking head): 'Ben is massively depressed. And he needs my help.'
jokes.setup: Ben has just excitedly shown Chris his claymation project insisting he's fine
jokes.punchline: Chris states the obvious diagnosis with total clinical confidence in the confessional, the comedy coming from how clear Ben's depression is to everyone but Ben
jokes.explanation: Effective mockumentary confessional beat. The gap between Ben's obliviousness and Chris's certainty is the joke. 'Massively' is a well-chosen intensifier — Chris never does anything by halves.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh, they're waving at us! Wave back!

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Andy, that's the police.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I know, they're being so nice!

jokes.text: See? There's more things to look at on the Internet besides naked guys, Ann.
jokes.setup: Leslie is complimenting Ann's research method (googling campaign managers)
jokes.punchline: Leslie parenthetically implies that Ann's internet usage is primarily for looking at naked men — delivered as a casual aside as if this is established fact
jokes.explanation: The joke works because of how matter-of-fact Leslie is — this is not an accusation, just a friendly reminder. Ann's confused 'What?' is the perfect response. Reveals Leslie's worldview in miniature: slightly oblivious, deeply earnest.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: The past is great! We had disco, we had the Concorde, we had The Twilight Zone...

dialogue.speaker: Pete
dialogue.line: Leslie, those aren't even—

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We also had Bigfoot, which may or may not have existed, but the *mystery* was incredible.

jokes.text: Is there even enough room for everyone? / Here. Sit on my lap. / No, that's humiliating. Can't I at least sit on Andy's lap? / No, that's Champion's spot. He called it.
jokes.setup: The team is crammed into the truck cab
jokes.punchline: Tom objects to sitting on a girl's lap as humiliating; April points out Champion has reserved Andy's lap; Ron orders Tom to sit on the girl's lap and 'be a man'
jokes.explanation: The escalation works well: each beat adds a layer of absurdity (Champion 'calling' the spot). Ron's command that Tom 'be a man and sit on that girl's lap' is a wonderfully Ron-twisted application of masculinity.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.line: You've violated several laws.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I don't see it as breaking the law. I see it as a philosophical disagreement with how the government has chosen to organize itself.

jokes.text: Champion is a way better kisser than you are, babe. / Uh-uh. Yes, he is. / He's even a better kisser than me. Here. Try some.
jokes.setup: Andy and April are in the truck with Champion the dog
jokes.punchline: Andy compares the dog's kissing favorably to both April and himself, then invites April to compare by kissing the dog — and April does it
jokes.explanation: Works because of how specific this is to Andy and April — this kind of affectionate weirdness is their relationship in miniature. The escalation from 'better than you' to 'better than me' to 'try some' is characteristic Andy logic.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Where are we?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: We're inside a building made of walls.

jokes.text: Ron honking the truck horn repeatedly near the hospital zone while insisting the police love them
jokes.setup: Andy suggests honking for the kids; a police siren sounds
jokes.punchline: Ron interprets the police siren as them 'sirening back to us' — a delightfully oblivious misread — and responds by honking more, doubling down
jokes.explanation: 'They're sirening back to us' is a great line — it reframes a threatening situation as a mutual greeting. Ron's subsequent honking ('Heard you, bud') is a perfect beat of compounding lawbreaking done with absolute confidence.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Pete, I need you to dunk at the rally. Look, I'm not asking you to do anything crazy. I'm not asking you to sleep with me or anything like that. Although if you wanted to, I mean, I wouldn't say no. But that's not what this is about. I just need you to dunk.

jokes.text: You can still dunk, right? / Oh, I can. But I won't.
jokes.setup: Ann is excited about Pistol Pete's planned dunk for the rally
jokes.punchline: Pete's response distinguishes 'can' from 'will' — he maintains his capability while asserting his choice with quiet dignity
jokes.explanation: Beautifully economical. Five words carry a lot: physical confidence ('I can'), philosophical objection ('but I won't'), and a hint of sadness about his identity. The comic timing of the pause implied by 'Oh, I can' before 'But I won't' is perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, you're not going to prostitute yourself for the campaign? I thought we were in this together, Ann.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Leslie, I never said I would do that.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, I'm hurt. I really thought you believed in this.

jokes.text: The past is great. The jitterbug, stagecoaches, Herman Munster.
jokes.setup: Pete says he doesn't want to live in the past; Leslie argues for the value of the past
jokes.punchline: Leslie's list of great things about the past is: the jitterbug (a dance), stagecoaches (a mode of transport), and Herman Munster (a fictional TV monster)
jokes.explanation: The list structure works because the items are simultaneously earnest and bizarre. Herman Munster is the kicker — it's deeply specific in an unexpected way. This is classic Leslie: passionate advocacy based on an oddly curated set of facts.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Pizza exists as Italian fast food.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: What? No it doesn't. I have no idea what you're talking about. Pizza? Never heard of it.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Now, if you'll excuse me, I need to get back to my calzone business.

jokes.text: As Peter Disellio, Regional Distributor for Derwin Ham Loafs.
jokes.setup: Pete says he'll endorse Leslie as himself
jokes.punchline: His current identity is 'Regional Distributor for Derwin Ham Loafs' — the specific product name doing a lot of comic work
jokes.explanation: The contrast between 'Pistol Pete' the legend and 'Peter Disellio, Regional Distributor for Derwin Ham Loafs' is perfectly deflating. 'Derwin Ham Loafs' as a product name is excellent Pawnee-universe absurdism.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: A calzone is just a pizza that's been folded in half. It's like your father's Oldsmobile, except it's a sandwich.

jokes.text: Officer, I've been operating heavy machinery since I was eight years old. Now, I respect you and your service to this town and your country. But what laws are we breaking exactly?
jokes.setup: Police have pulled over the overloaded truck; Ron is facing the officer
jokes.punchline: Ron establishes his credentials (operating machinery since age 8), offers sincere respect for service, then — with complete good faith — asks which specific laws they've violated, implying he doesn't think any have been broken
jokes.explanation: The character integration here is exceptional — this is Ron's entire libertarian worldview in three sentences. He respects authority as people while fundamentally challenging their right to govern. The 'since I was eight' establishes that Ron considers his experience a valid credential against state oversight. The comedy of the officer then listing six obvious violations is perfectly set up.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I'm starting a business called... Bed Bath & Beyond Burgers.

jokes.text: The officer lists six violations. Ron's response: 'Okay. Well, we have a philosophical difference on what constitutes a law.'
jokes.setup: The officer has listed: four people in front seat, no seatbelts, speeding, horn through hospital zone, open rear with falling debris, no commercial license
jokes.punchline: Ron's response to six clearly-stated laws is to reframe all of them as a 'philosophical difference' — as if legality is a matter of opinion
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best Ron joke and one of his all-time great lines. After genuinely asking which laws they broke and being given a comprehensive list, Ron reframes ALL OF IT as a 'philosophical difference on what constitutes a law.' The character integration is as high as it gets — this is Ron Swanson's entire ideology in eleven words. The economy is perfect. It would be quoted for years. Earns an 8.7 craft score by being genuinely comparable to the 8.0 anchor example in its sharpness and character specificity, exceeding it in quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: So here's my idea: a chain of restaurants where all the food is served at exactly body temperature, and the waiters only communicate through interpretive dance.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Ben, that is literally the most innovative concept I have ever heard. This is going to be huge. I'm talking Fortune 500. I'm talking about changing the entire restaurant industry. The synergy alone is going to be off the charts. This is a home run. Actually, it's beyond a home run. It's a grand slam in the bottom of the ninth with two outs. I can already see the IPO. We're going to make millions. Billions, even. This is the best idea anyone has ever had, ever, in the history of ideas.

jokes.text: April's location response when Leslie asks where they are: 'My mother's butt.'
jokes.setup: Leslie urgently asks April where they are so she can come get them
jokes.punchline: April gives a deliberately useless answer — 'my mother's butt' — with apparent complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: Classic April obstructionism. Even in a crisis she won't give a straight answer. The childish insult ('my mother's butt') is deliberately juvenile, which is the joke — April defaults to playground-level unhelpfulness under pressure. Character-specific but not a sophisticated joke.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: That was the greatest idea I've ever heard.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I have no idea what they're talking about. I wasn't listening at all.

jokes.text: Men in uniform love me.
jokes.setup: Leslie is heading to spring the team from police custody
jokes.punchline: Her confidence is stated as established fact with zero supporting evidence in the scene
jokes.explanation: Brief but effective Leslie confidence moment. Economy is excellent (four words), though the joke is a touch generic compared to the episode's best.

dialogue.speaker: Police Officer
dialogue.line: April sicced the three-legged dog on a police officer

jokes.text: Yeah, anything short of sexual favors. What? I do not... I repeat, I do not want you to tempt him with sexual favors. I wasn't going to. Good. I wouldn't, either. That's where I draw the line. Although, I am a little offended that you wouldn't do that.
jokes.setup: Leslie tells Ann to do 'whatever it takes' to get Pete to dunk
jokes.punchline: The conversation spirals from Leslie disclaiming sexual favors, to Ann defending herself, to Leslie being slightly offended Ann wouldn't consider it — inverting the moral position completely
jokes.explanation: The escalation is well-crafted: Leslie raises sexual favors only to disclaim them, then keeps disclaiming while making it awkward, then closes with a joke that cuts against her own position. The final beat of being offended Ann wouldn't do it subverts the expected moral lecturing and shows Leslie's complex priorities.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm calling this dysfunctional group my essential campaign team.

jokes.text: Ben: 'Pizza? Never heard of it. That's what people will be saying in 20 years. Because pizza is old news, Chris. Pizza is your grandfather's calzone.'
jokes.setup: Chris points out that pizza is already an Italian fast food option
jokes.punchline: Ben dismisses pizza's existence, predicts its obsolescence, then reframes calzones (the derived food) as the original — inverting culinary history
jokes.explanation: Pizza is your grandfather's calzone' is genuinely inspired — it flips the obvious relationship between pizza and calzone, and it's the kind of thing a depressed person with too much time would convince themselves of. The grandiosity of Ben's Fast-Casual Italian vision while making calzones alone in his apartment is beautifully tragic-comic. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Pistol Pete
dialogue.line: You know, I've spent my whole life being defined by one moment on the basketball court. But I've realized that life is like basketball in reverse—you start out getting fouled constantly, nobody passes to you, and by the time you finally learn the rules, the game's almost over.

jokes.text: Ben announces 'The Low-Cal Calzone Zone.' Chris: 'That idea is literally the greatest idea I have ever heard in my life.' Leslie (via phone screen, implied): 'That idea is terrible.'
jokes.setup: Ben has been pitching his Italian fast-casual restaurant concept to increasingly enthusiastic Chris
jokes.punchline: The name is revealed — 'The Low-Cal Calzone Zone' — and the immediate split reaction (Chris's hyperbolic praise vs. off-screen dismissal) frames it perfectly. The name is funny for being both terrible and oddly catchy.
jokes.explanation: The Low-Cal Calzone Zone is one of Parks and Rec's most beloved jokes — it became a genuine cultural reference. The name is funny on its own (the triple-rhyme sounds both professional and absurd), Chris's superlative praise makes it funnier, and the immediate dismissal provides the punchline. The joke works because Ben's depression has channeled into something so specific and so him. This earns its high scores — it's comparable to the 8.0 anchor example in quotability and exceeds it.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Ben, I think you need help.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Help with what? My interpretive dance-boxing hybrid? Because I've been working on some really innovative moves.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: No, Ben. I'm talking about your depression.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Oh. Well, that too, I guess.

jokes.text: Len, you're killing me. They broke about 50 laws, Knope. And that girl, she tried to get that gimp dog to bite me.
jokes.setup: Leslie arrives at the police stop and tries to charm the officer into releasing her team
jokes.punchline: The officer's report includes April apparently weaponizing Champion the three-legged dog — a detail that (a) confirms April's character and (b) makes the situation more absurd
jokes.explanation: April trying to sic a three-legged dog on a police officer is exactly in character and plays as a reveal about what happened off-screen. The barking sound effect after the mention is a nice comedic beat.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I'm fine. Look, I made this claymation video of a little guy walking around.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: See? Totally fine.

jokes.text: Leslie negotiating with officer: 'You and I both know that you'd rather go home to Deborah, have a nice home-cooked meal, and do what comes naturally.' Officer: 'That's not appropriate.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to charm the officer into dropping the charges
jokes.punchline: Leslie's 'men in uniform love me' approach involves weirdly intimate knowledge of the officer's home life and a suggestive phrase that she is apparently oblivious to
jokes.explanation: The callback to Leslie's confidence about men in uniform pays off — it turns out her charm offensive is weird and boundary-crossing. The officer's dry 'That's not appropriate' is the perfect underplayed response.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Champion needs to use the bathroom.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: He's going to poop in the car.

jokes.text: Ann's emotional conversation with Pistol Pete: 'Sometimes, life dunks you.' (Long beat.)
jokes.setup: Ann has gotten Pete talking about his feelings about his basketball legacy in an attempt to convince him to dunk at the rally
jokes.punchline: Pete arrives at a profound-sounding life metaphor — 'Sometimes, life dunks you' — that is both emotionally resonant and absurd given the literal context
jokes.explanation: The double meaning of 'dunk' makes this work — it's a real emotional statement that is also inadvertently the thing Ann wants Pete to do. The line is quotable and lands as both genuine and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I compared three seconds of my amateur claymation to a blockbuster movie with a $200 million budget.

jokes.text: Chris tries to get Ben to jog. Ben: 'Oh, no thanks, Chris. I'm kind of tearing this claymation video a new one right now.'
jokes.setup: Chris is concerned about Ben and suggests a jog to get endorphins going
jokes.punchline: Ben uses aggressive creative slang ('tearing it a new one') to describe his claymation hobby — the violent idiom applied to craft-time is funny, and the oblivious confidence about his clearly mediocre work amplifies it
jokes.explanation: The dissonance between the aggressive phrase and the sad hobby is the gag. Setup for the claymation reveal payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: April, what's the status on the basketball-themed rally venue?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Well, we have a problem. You can't have a basketball event in a basketball court because of the basketball.

jokes.text: Chris: 'You are wildly, insanely depressed.' Ben: 'Depressed? I'm the furthest thing from depressed. I mean, look at what I've accomplished. Do you see him? Do you think a depressed person could make this?'
jokes.setup: Chris directly confronts Ben about his depression; Ben denies it and gestures to his claymation figure as evidence of his mental health
jokes.punchline: Ben's proof that he's not depressed is the claymation figure — which we and Chris can see is not an impressive defense
jokes.explanation: The dramatic gesture to the clearly unimpressive claymation is a good visual comedy beat. Ben's complete sincerity makes it work — he genuinely doesn't see the irony.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: He told me to read the contract, but he said it in a condescending tone, so I didn't. That's on him.

jokes.text: Ben says 'With my claymaish?' when Chris says he needs help with his life.
jokes.setup: Chris says Ben needs help; Ben assumes Chris is referring to the claymation
jokes.punchline: 'Claymaish' — Ben apparently can't even say the full word 'claymation' correctly, suggesting his mastery of the hobby is even less than we thought
jokes.explanation: A small but charming detail — the mispronunciation/truncation 'claymaish' suggests either Ben is going native with his hobby or he just can't quite commit to the word. Either way it's endearing and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I Jetsoned your poster. Like the cartoon family, but as a verb.

jokes.text: Pete tells Ann about his strict religious upbringing: 'But that's what life is like in a strict Roman Catholic household. Of course, my father, he was more stick than carrot, when it came to matters of discipline.'
jokes.setup: Ann has gotten Pete deeply into his emotional backstory while trying to secure the dunk; his father's strictness is now on the table
jokes.punchline: The incongruity of this level of personal disclosure in what was supposed to be a quick celeb endorsement meeting, plus the formal phrasing 'more stick than carrot' for a childhood trauma
jokes.explanation: The situational comedy of Ann having opened a therapy session she can't close is funny, but Pete's specific lines here aren't especially sharp. The 'stick than carrot' phrasing is nice but the overall beat is more setup than payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: You know, this poster really reminds me of the principles of brutalism in urban design. The way the negative space interacts with the compositional elements... it's quite striking, actually.

jokes.text: Ben shows Chris his claymation. It plays for about ten seconds, stops, restarts for a few more seconds. 'Did you pause it?' 'No. Hang on.' It plays a few more seconds. Stops. 'Oh, my God. That's the whole thing. That's three weeks of work.'
jokes.setup: Ben has been hyping his claymation for the whole episode, comparing it to Avatar in an email to Leslie
jokes.punchline: The video plays twice, stops, restarts — and the whole thing is perhaps 20 seconds of animation. Three weeks of work.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's comedic climax for the Ben storyline and one of its highest-impact moments. The structure is exceptional: the whole episode has been building up Ben's investment in this project. The false start (viewers and Chris think the video ended, Ben assures them it just paused) and then the actual end — which is barely longer — is perfectly staged cringe. 'That's three weeks of work' is the devastating punchline that lands hard. The earned_vs_cheap score is a 9 because the whole episode has been working toward this reveal and it does not cheat — the absurdity is proportionate to the buildup. Comparable to the 9.5 anchor in its structural payoff, though the moment is character-specific rather than universal.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I got Pete to come to the rally.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's amazing! How did you do it?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Well, we were both crying.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Why were you crying?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I don't know why Pete was crying.

jokes.text: Ben: 'I e-mailed Leslie two days ago and I compared it to Avatar, Chris.'
jokes.setup: Ben is now fully confronting the reality of his claymation
jokes.punchline: He compared a ~20-second claymation video to Avatar — one of the highest-grossing films of all time — in an email to Leslie
jokes.explanation: This topper to the claymation reveal is excellent. The Avatar comparison is the perfect escalation — it's the most grandiose possible comparison for the most pathetically small product. The fact that he sent it to Leslie in writing makes the shame more concrete and funnier. Earns its high score as a callback that genuinely escalates the original joke.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Jerry, what did you do? I was going to cancel this thing!

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I just made some calls, got some people interested—

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Interested?! There are a hundred people here! A hundred! Do you understand what you've done? I had a whole plan to shut this down gracefully, and now I have to actually run a rally!

jokes.text: April (confessional): 'The stupid guy I called to book this place didn't tell me they took off the basketball floor for a hockey game. Or maybe he did tell me, but he was so stupid and boring that I wasn't listening. And, either way, it was his fault, because he was stupid and I hated him.'
jokes.setup: The venue has been converted to an ice skating rink; Leslie needs to know why
jokes.punchline: April's explanation pivots from blaming the guy to admitting she might not have been listening, to re-blaming him on the grounds that he was 'stupid and boring'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best character comedy moments. The structure of the explanation is perfect: blame, self-incriminating admission, re-blame on circular grounds. 'Either way, it was his fault, because he was stupid and I hated him' is a genuinely wonderful line — April's logic is internally consistent in the most irresponsible way possible. The character integration is a 9 because this is April's entire work ethic condensed into one confession.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ladies and gentlemen, I present to you... a red carpet entrance!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Now, I know what you're thinking: 'Tom, this is only three feet long.' And you're right. But that's three feet of *premium* red carpet. It's like a red carpet, but concentrated. It's red carpet essence.

jokes.text: Ron presents the stage: it is comically tiny. 'Good Lord. What happened to the rest of my face?' / 'We had to Jetsons most of the poster, too. But I kind of like it.'
jokes.setup: Wood had to be jettisoned from the truck (falling debris violation); Ron built the stage with what remained
jokes.punchline: The stage is tiny; the Leslie poster has been cut down to just a portion of her face. Ron is unbothered and claims to like the partial portrait.
jokes.explanation: A strong visual gag — the tiny stage and cropped poster are perfect physical comedy payoffs for the earlier truck debris scene. Ron's deadpan 'I kind of like it' followed by the bizarre non-sequitur 'because windows are the eyes to the house' is wonderfully bizarre. High impact because it's a visual reveal.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I have no idea what just happened, but I'm going to assume this is the dog's fault.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: And now it's peeing on me.

jokes.text: Ron: 'Because windows are the eyes to the house.'
jokes.setup: Ron has just said he likes the partial Leslie poster; this is his stated reason
jokes.punchline: The justification for liking the cropped poster is a completely unrelated aphorism about windows and houses that makes no sense in context
jokes.explanation: Ron's non-sequitur wisdom — dispensed with complete confidence — is a comedic signature. The line sounds like something that should mean something but applied here means nothing at all. The delivery of this by Nick Offerman would be perfectly solemn. Very quotable precisely because it sounds profound and isn't.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ron, how am I supposed to get up there?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You jump.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: It's like eight feet high.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Then I suggest you jump higher.

jokes.text: Ann's report on Pete: 'Right now, he's curled up in the back seat of my car, talking about his father, who was a piece of work. I actually think he did the best he could for a single father, but I may be too close to the situation.'
jokes.setup: Leslie asks if Pete is going to dunk
jokes.punchline: Ann has gotten so absorbed in Pete's backstory therapy session that she's formed her own opinion about his father's parenting and is worried about her objectivity
jokes.explanation: A great joke about Ann's nurse-mode empathy overtaking her campaign-manager role. 'I may be too close to the situation' — after knowing Pete for 20 minutes — is wonderfully oblivious. The character integration is strong: Ann's warmth is both her greatest asset and her greatest professional liability.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: This tastes like a belt.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: That's because it's from my herb belt.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: No, I mean it literally tastes like a belt. Like, a leather belt.

jokes.text: Ann: 'Is he going to dunk for me?' / Leslie: 'I'm not sure. I couldn't hear through all the crying.' / Leslie: 'He's crying?' / Ann: 'No, I was crying. It's been a stressful day, and he's had a really rough life.'
jokes.setup: Leslie asks if Pete will dunk; Ann says she couldn't hear through all the crying
jokes.punchline: The crying was ANN's, not Pete's — and her justification ('it's been a stressful day, and he's had a really rough life') treats her own emotional breakdown as a reasonable response
jokes.explanation: Excellent misdirection followed by a reveal that's funnier than what we expected. The setup implies Pete is having an emotional breakdown; the punchline is that Ann is the one who broke down. Her calm justification — delivered as if this is completely reasonable — is perfect. The double-beat ('it's been a stressful day' AND 'he's had a really rough life') shows Ann genuinely feels both reasons justify her crying.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Ben's been really withdrawn lately. He won't go to meetings, he's stopped color-coding his binders, and worst of all, he called a fun meeting 'a waste of time.'

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I'm worried he's depressed.

jokes.text: Leslie asks Jerry to report on the crowd, hoping he 'pulled a Jerry' and no one showed up. Jerry: 'First of all, I don't like it when you guys use that term.' Then confirms there are 100 people.
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to find a way to cancel the disastrous rally; she hopes Jerry has failed at his one job
jokes.punchline: Jerry objects mildly to the term 'pulled a Jerry' — then immediately proves himself by having actually done his job, making his protest doubly pathetic
jokes.explanation: A classic Jerry joke structure: his dignified objection to being a punchline is immediately undercut by his competence being a problem. Tom's 'Can't you do anything wrong, Jerry?' is the perfect topper.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We need to fight childhood obesity by encouraging exercise and healthy eating.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We need to fight children.

jokes.text: Tom: 'Yeah, can't you do anything wrong, Jerry?'
jokes.setup: Jerry has just done his job correctly, which is inconvenient
jokes.punchline: Tom expresses genuine frustration that Jerry succeeded — inverting the usual direction of criticism
jokes.explanation: The inversion of the usual dynamic — criticizing Jerry for doing his job — is sharp. Short, punchy, high economy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, so the rally didn't go exactly as planned. But I want to assure everyone that my campaign is going to be very interesting.

jokes.text: The rally entrance: triumphant music plays, the team walks out onto what is now an ice rink. Tom stops mid-red-carpet because it runs out. 'I couldn't afford enough premium carpet to get us to the stage. I mean, it was a short walk, but it was pretty luxurious, right?'
jokes.setup: The team is making their big triumphant entrance to energetic music; Tom has laid red carpet for the walk
jokes.punchline: The red carpet ends well before the stage; Tom defends its partial luxury with characteristic shamelessness
jokes.explanation: The visual payoff of the red carpet ending mid-walk is excellent physical comedy. Tom's unbothered defense — 'it was pretty luxurious, right?' — is peak Tom. The callback to his red carpet obsession pays off.

dialogue.speaker: Pete
dialogue.line: I'm going to dunk it!

dialogue.speaker: Narrator
dialogue.line: [Pete attempts the dunk and fails badly]

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That was... a really creative approach to basketball!

jokes.text: Andy slips and falls on the ice rink while trying to walk to the stage, bringing down the entrance music.
jokes.setup: The team is trying to walk across what is now an ice rink with no skates
jokes.punchline: Andy falls, the music stops, chaos ensues as the rally entrance collapses
jokes.explanation: A visual/physical comedy moment that plays better on screen than in transcript. The impact is high because it's the first domino in the rally disaster sequence. The stopped music is a great comedic beat.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We have Tom, who's great at social media but once tweeted a picture of his foot thinking it was a meme. We have Donna, who organized our entire volunteer database in Excel but refuses to learn what a cloud is. We have Jerry, who shows up to every meeting 20 minutes late with the wrong coffee order, but somehow always has the exact statistic we need. And we have April, who communicates exclusively through sighs and eye rolls, yet somehow convinced the entire Parks Department to volunteer for my campaign. That's our team. Perfectly summarizes their incompetent enthusiasm.

jokes.text: Ron is holding Champion the dog while the team scrambles on the ice. Champion begins urinating. 'He is peeing. He is now peeing. Now, I'm putting him down.' 'No, Ron! He only has three legs!'
jokes.setup: Ron is holding Champion while trying to manage the chaos of the rally entrance on the ice
jokes.punchline: Champion urinates on Ron; Ron announces his intention to set him down; April objects on disability grounds as if the ice would be more dangerous than the peeing
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'Andy fell' to 'dog is peeing on Ron' to 'April won't let Ron put the peeing dog down because of his disability' is genuinely funny. April's logic — protecting Champion from ice at the cost of Ron's dignity — is perfect character comedy. 'He is peeing. He is NOW peeing.' as a Ron announcement is great deadpan.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa. What is happening here? Are you two...? Oh man, this is so beautiful. Even the dog gets it.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Look at him. He's like, 'Finally, my parents are back together.'

jokes.text: Leslie: 'Ron? Ron? There's no stairs. How do I get onto the stage?' (music stops) (thud/stumble implied)
jokes.setup: The tiny stage Ron built has no stairs; Leslie can't get onto it
jokes.punchline: The music stops as Leslie faces this completely foreseeable but unaddressed logistical problem — another layer of the rally disaster
jokes.explanation: The visual of Leslie being unable to mount a comically small stage during an already-chaotic entrance is strong physical comedy. Another well-earned escalation beat in the rally disaster sequence.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I'm married.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No, you're not.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Yes, I am.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ann, you're not married.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I am married!

jokes.text: Ann attempts to get onto the stage — grunting is heard, music restarts and stops. Ann eventually makes it up with effort. 'Mmm!'
jokes.setup: The stage has no stairs and is on an ice rink; Ann is trying to mount it
jokes.punchline: It takes Ann multiple attempts, accompanied by grunting, to get onto a stage that should be simple to climb — all while triumphant music keeps starting and stopping
jokes.explanation: The stopping and restarting music is the real joke here — the technical direction keeps trying to be triumphant and failing along with the characters. Solid physical comedy that reads better visually.

jokes.text: Chris gives Ben a herbal smoothie. Ben: 'It tastes like a belt.' Chris: 'I know. Isn't it awful? But it works wonderfully.'
jokes.setup: Chris has made Ben a special herb smoothie from his 'herb belt' to help with his depression
jokes.punchline: Ben's taste assessment is 'it tastes like a belt' — not a specific food, but a leather accessory; Chris agrees it's awful while endorsing it
jokes.explanation: A great small joke. 'It tastes like a belt' is a very specific and funny descriptor — not unpleasant food flavors like 'dirt' or 'medicine' but a manufactured object. Chris enthusiastically agreeing it's awful while defending it is perfect character comedy.

jokes.text: Chris: 'Drink up. Because it has every herb in my herb belt.'
jokes.setup: Chris is administering care to depressed Ben
jokes.punchline: The existence of an 'herb belt' — a belt worn specifically to carry herbs — is the joke; Chris has an actual belt for this purpose
jokes.explanation: The herb belt is a perfect Chris detail — it implies a whole lifestyle commitment. The casual way he introduces it ('every herb IN my herb belt') suggests this is normal to him. High character integration because this is exactly the kind of object only Chris would own and deploy.

jokes.text: Chris diagnoses what made him realize Ben was depressed: 'The Letters to Cleo T-shirt, the unshaven face, the Doc Martens... And your hair does not have that normal uptight, rigid, inflexible Ben Wyatt sense of fun.'
jokes.setup: Ben asks how Chris knew he was depressed
jokes.punchline: Chris lists external indicators including Ben's hair not having its 'uptight, rigid, inflexible sense of fun' — an oxymoron that perfectly captures Chris's earnest observation style
jokes.explanation: The phrase 'uptight, rigid, inflexible Ben Wyatt sense of fun' is genuinely funny — it's three negative adjectives applied to 'fun' by someone trying to be complementary. Chris means it as a fond description of Ben's personality while inadvertently describing him as deeply un-fun. The Letters to Cleo T-shirt as a depression signal is also great specificity.

jokes.text: Leslie at the podium: 'Together, we can defeat... obese children.' (card disorder) 'I'm sure that was something positive, originally.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is giving her rally speech; her index cards got out of order when they fell
jokes.punchline: Reading from the wrong card, she announces a campaign goal to 'defeat obese children' — then narrates her own mistake with complete composure
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's strongest jokes. 'Together, we can defeat obese children' is an extraordinary accidental political statement, and the recovery line 'I'm sure that was something positive, originally' shows Leslie's unflappable character — she identifies and contextualizes her mistake without losing dignity. The economy is excellent. Highly quotable and deserves its high scores.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'This is just a disaster, isn't it? This is the... This is the worst political event ever in history.' / Leslie: 'Well, I can assure you people in the bleachers that if you follow my campaign, it will be interesting.'
jokes.setup: The rally has gone catastrophically wrong; Leslie acknowledges it from the podium
jokes.punchline: Her pivot from honest disaster admission to a campaign promise of 'interesting' (the absolute floor of political promises) is perfectly calibrated — and delivered directly to 'people in the bleachers' as if addressing a specific demographic
jokes.explanation: The best Leslie moment in the episode might be this one. After an episode of mounting disaster, her offer of 'interesting' as a campaign promise is both deflating and strangely inspiring. The specificity of 'people in the bleachers' as an address is a great detail that suggests Leslie's political brain is still running even in total failure.

jokes.text: Pistol Pete endorses Leslie, says 'a vote for her is a slam dunk,' then attempts a dunk on the ice... and falls spectacularly.
jokes.setup: Pete has spent the whole episode refusing to dunk the ball; he relents for the endorsement
jokes.punchline: He uses the 'slam dunk' punchline verbally (which pays off the whole running negotiation) — then actually attempts it on ice, with predictable results
jokes.explanation: The structural payoff of the Pistol Pete arc is excellent. The verbal 'slam dunk' delivers the episode-long setup while the actual physical attempt — doomed to fail on an ice rink — is the perfect slapstick topper. Leslie's 'Pistol Pete, everybody. Still got it.' is a beautifully deadpan cap. This moment earns a 9.0 impact score because it resolves two narrative threads simultaneously in the funniest way possible.

jokes.text: Leslie asks Ben to be her campaign manager. Chris: 'You know, Leslie, Ben's really been going through something. And he's on a journey, so I don't think he's going to be taking the first job...' Ben: 'I'll do it. I'm in. I've done enough exploring. I'm good.'
jokes.setup: Chris has spent the whole episode trying to help Ben through his depression by supporting his hobbies
jokes.punchline: The instant Leslie offers a real job, Ben abandons all of Chris's careful work in one second, completely undercutting everything Chris just said mid-sentence
jokes.explanation: A great payoff for the Ben depression arc. Chris's gentle protective speech is interrupted the moment a real opportunity appears. 'I've done enough exploring. I'm good.' — delivered after maybe 30 seconds of deliberation — is perfectly Ben: competent, practical, and deeply aware of his own needs once someone offers him structure.

jokes.text: Ann is fired. Ann: 'Oh, thank God.'
jokes.setup: Leslie fires Ann as campaign manager to hire Ben
jokes.punchline: Ann's response is immediate, unguarded relief — she wanted out
jokes.explanation: Callbacks to the opening beats of the episode. Ann's 'Oh, thank God' is a great button — it resolves the arc that started with Leslie hiring her against her will. The economy is near-perfect for what it accomplishes.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'Oh! Don't make out. It's making Champion sad.'
jokes.setup: Ben and Leslie reunite and presumably kiss/embrace after she hires him
jokes.punchline: Leslie's objection to their celebration isn't professionalism or appropriateness — it's Champion the three-legged dog's emotional state
jokes.explanation: A neat callback to Champion and a funny final note on the romantic reunion. Leslie's concern for Champion's feelings above all else is both absurd and characteristically warm.

jokes.text: The team gives Pete cookies and balloons as apology for 'dredging up your past just to be publicly humiliated.' Pete: 'That's nice.' / 'Is there anything else we can do?' Pete: 'You can let me take you to dinner.' Andy/April: 'Yes, Ann. Yes, you should do that.' Ann: 'Oh, I can't, though. Because I'm married.' Andy/April: 'You're not married.' Ann: 'She's not married.'
jokes.setup: Pete is given a sweet apology gift; offered anything else he wants; he asks Ann to dinner
jokes.punchline: Ann's reflexive objection that she's married is immediately corrected by multiple people — she's not married, and has apparently forgotten this — followed by Pete's (or April's) dry 'This is uncomfortable'
jokes.explanation: A great closing scene beat. Ann's 'I'm married' as an excuse is both a character tell (her avoidance instincts) and a factual error, corrected immediately by everyone around her. 'This is uncomfortable' as the closing line is perfectly understated. The scene wraps with cringe and warmth simultaneously.

jokes.text: 'This is uncomfortable.'
jokes.setup: Ann has been publicly corrected that she is not married, while a man is asking her on a date in front of the whole group
jokes.punchline: 'This is uncomfortable' — delivered with what must be perfect deadpan after an already-uncomfortable social situation
jokes.explanation: Three words that serve as a perfect episode button. The economy score is a 10 — it says everything that needs to be said. Not the most original construction but the delivery in context lands cleanly.

tmdb_overview: Leslie enlists everyone's help in staging an attention-getting event. Ben takes up a new hobby, while April and Andy adopt a pet.
insight: Leslie's comeback narrative finds footing through character-driven absurdism despite mid-tier humor scores.
